passage: The tyre swing hung from the big neem tree behind the panchayat school, and the bell for the end of lunch would ring soon. Anirban had waited through three turns, counting the pushes under his breath. When the girl before him jumped off, he stepped forward, but Jeevan slid past him and dropped into the tyre, grinning. Heat rushed up Anirban's neck. His fists closed. "That's mine!" he shouted, so loudly that two goats by the wall lifted their heads. Jeevan blinked. "I didn't see you." Anirban didn't believe a word. He was certain Jeevan had watched him waiting and cut in anyway, just to win. Then the bell began to ring.

qa.a: It hung from the big neem tree behind the panchayat school.

qa.q: What did Anirban feel sure of when Jeevan got on the swing?
qa.a: He was certain Jeevan had watched him waiting and cut in just to win, even though Jeevan said, "I didn't see you."

qa.a: Jeevan looks surprised and says they didn't see Anirban, so the shout may feel like an attack out of nowhere and make Jeevan want to defend too.

passage: Rain had left puddles under the climbing frame, so only one swing in the little park behind the apartment blocks in Porto was dry. Gabriel had been saving that swing in his head all afternoon. He wiped the seat with his sleeve, turned to wave at his dad on the bench, and when he turned back, Nadia was sitting on it, feet already off the ground. Something hot flashed in his chest. "That's mine!" he yelled, much louder than he meant, and his dad looked up from his phone. Nadia dragged her shoes to stop. "You weren't on it." "I wiped it! You saw me!" Gabriel was sure she had waited for him to look away. His face burned, and he planted himself in front of the swing so she couldn't go higher.

qa.a: Nadia may feel accused and startled, because from her side the swing was empty, so she is likely to start defending herself.

passage: Sit, Vikas. You think your Dadi never fought? When I was nine, Sunaina and I quarrelled over a skipping rope in the lane behind the mill. "You lost the whole game because you're a baby," Binita said. "Even Mumma says you can't lose properly."
"I'm not a baby." Tenzin's voice shook.
"Baby, baby. Look, his ears have gone red."
"Stop it!"
"Why? You always—"
"STOP!" Tenzin's hands felt hot, and his heart thumped so hard he could hear it. He shoved the board, and the pieces flew across the rug.
"Mumma! He threw everything!"
Mumma came in from the kitchen. "Tenzin—"
But Tenzin was already running to the bedroom. The door banged. Inside, he sat against the bed, breathing fast, face burning, not even sure what he had just done.
"He always does this," Binita said.
"Let him breathe first," Mumma said quietly.

passage: Last week I cried in the art room, and I still don't really know how it happened. I'm ten, and I hadn't cried at school since I was a small boy. Kashish kept laughing at my drawing of a horse. "It looks like a dog with a long neck," Kashish said, and then everybody at our table started saying it. I tried to say something clever back. But my heart was going so fast, and my face got so hot, that my brain just went blank. No words came. Tears came instead, big ones, in front of everyone. I pushed my chair back and walked out to the corridor. I didn't decide to. My legs just went. passage: Rain had pushed the whole PE class into the school hall, where forty children were shouting over the thunder. In one corner, Preeti and Vijay were nose to nose over the one dry football, Vijay's fists clenched, Preeti close to tears. Mrs D'Souza didn't ask who started it. She stepped between them. "Vijay, fill your bottle at the cooler and walk back slowly. Preeti, sit by the window with me and take ten slow breaths." The buses were due in fifteen minutes, and she could easily have made a quick ruling. She waited instead. When Vijay came back with his shoulders down, she asked each of them what had happened, and then, "What were you feeling right then?"

passage: The tuition room in Manjula Miss's Jayanagar flat was small, and the fight over the shared ruler filled it. Shreya had snapped it; Nitin said she did it on purpose; Shreya called him a liar. Manjula Miss put down her chai. "Right. No one is in trouble. Shreya, walk out to the balcony and water the tulsi. Nitin, drink this glass of water, slowly." Neither child moved at first. Then Shreya stomped out, and Nitin gulped, then sipped. Two minutes passed. The traffic horns below filled the silence. When Shreya came back, her breathing had slowed. Manjula Miss sat between them. "Now. Tell me what happened, one at a time. And tell me how it felt inside."

"One minute, Maria di. Look, forty-two people have seen it."
Maria sat beside her sister on the sofa. The class chat was scrolling by itself. "Who's Khushi?"

qa.q: What could Fardeen try so he can go first without feeling he lost?
qa.a: He could message Dilnaz privately, say the laughing got to him and ask to reset, which is a strong move, not a defeat.

qa.q: How might Maria see things if she knew the laughing was the real hurt?
qa.a: Maria might feel sorry and realise the audience made it worse, and could choose not to join in next time.

grounding: Shows a teen whose anger drains after a day of sulking, seeing that being laughed at hurt most, and wondering how to step back without looking weak.
